newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Saudis at OPEC renew call for higher oil price.
newsitem.headline: Saudis at OPEC renew call for higher oil price.

text.p: Saudi Arabia reiterated ahead of OPEC talks in Vienna on Wednesday that it wants to see higher oil prices.

But it was not immediately clear what success, if any, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries was having in efforts to get its biggest quota violator, Venezuela, to curb excess production to help achieve a stronger market.
OPEC was opening Vienna talks to assign production quotas for the six months from July 1.
Delegates forecast that a Saudi-backed majority would favour the expedient of a freeze of current quotas under the current ceiling of 25 million barrels per day until year's end.

But Iran, with the Saudis' support, led a move to try to deal with the chronic quota violations by some of the 11 members, led by Venezuela, that have driven actual OPEC output up some two million barrels above the target.
Excess oil has already sent prices down to around $18 per barrel, from $25 at the end of 1996.
"Yes, we would like to see the price higher;" Oil Minister Ali Naimi of Saudi Arabia, the OPEC linchpin, told lobby reporters.
OPEC decided that all 11 heads of delegation would meet in closed "consultative" session at 1500 GMT in the hotel suite of the cartel president, Abdullah al-Badri of Libya.
This varied a previous schedule which was for the conference to begin on Wednesday afternoon with the usual plenary at the offices of its Vienna-based secretariat.

Venezuela's minister, Erwin Arrieta, was earlier called to a private session with Badri, Ali Naimi of Saudi Arabia and Gholamrezah Aghazadeh of Iran - which a Gulf delegate said was intended to "emphasise the need for quota compliance".
That sounded like OPEC parlance for a tongue lashing. But beyond that, OPEC has no mechanism to compel a sovereign state to honour its quotas.
Delegates said that Saudi Arabia seemed in no mood to threaten to turn up the taps on its huge spare capacity as a retaliatory measure.
"There is no warning," said a Gulf source who stressed that an appeal was being made to "common interest". But Venezuela is ready to argue that the entire quota system is flawed.
Petroleos de Venezuela, their state oil company, has said that OPEC should abandon quotas altogether and opt for a policy of expanding its share of the world market.
That view is also being aired among analysts of the market.
"OPEC is at risk of being an anachronism," says Geoff Pyne, an energy economist at UBS Ltd. "It is achieving the status of a gentlemen's club with almost no influence on oil prices."
"It's a fantasy world. The quota system is a mechanism for losing their share of the market".

Pyne argued that OPEC output curbs, albeit leaky, do suffice to keep a floor under prices. But that simply ensures that others can turn a profit by investing in new oil fields to poach its market from it.
